newsitem.title: CONGO: Mobutu on board for Zaire talks, rebels mass forces.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu on board for Zaire talks, rebels mass forces.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko boarded a South African navy ship in Congo on Friday for talks with his civil war rival Laurent Kabila, witnesses said.

Mobutu, one of Africa's last veteran strongmen but whose grip on Zaire is crumbling after three decades in power, went onto the Russian-built ice-breaker five hours late after poor health prevented him climbing 31 steep metal steps to board.
In the event, he was driven up a make-shift ramp onto the SAS Outeniqua, where South Africa's Nelson Mandela was waiting to host the talks.
The Outeniqua then left port at 5:20 p.m. (1620 GMT), sailing towards international waters off the Angola-Zaire border to pick up Kabila.

As Mobutu waited in Congo's port of Pointe Noire where the Outeniqua was moored, Kabila's rebels flew troops, artillery and other supplies towards the forward base which is a springboard for their march on the capital Kinshasa.
On the humanitarian front, an airlift to repatriate up to 100,000 sick and dying Rwandan Hutu refugees from northeastern Zaire gathered pace.

"We are dealing with two outstanding leaders who are conscious of the importance of an amicable settlement which will satisfy both of them as well as the people of Zaire," Mandela told reporters on the Russian-built Outeniqua earlier.
"I am confident the two leaders realise the importance of a peaceful settlement," he said. "I know few leaders who have made military gains and nevertheless been committed to peace as Mr Kabila has."

Officials said Kabila had been waiting in Angola's capital Luanda. He and Mandela's deputy Thabo Mbeki were to take a helicopter to join Mobutu and Mandela on the Outeniqua in international waters off Soyo by the Angolan-Zaire border.
But some officials said Kabila may join the ship sooner.
"We are prepared to stay on that ship as long as it takes to reach some conclusions," Mbeki told reporters in Luanda.
Mobutu, 66, has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but prostate cancer and the whirlwind rebel offensive have weakened his grip on power.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis living there, control about three quarters of Zaire.
Kabila, 56, says Mobutu must stand down and has refused to declare a truce for the talks.
Confusion over timing has plagued the runup to the meeting, which diplomats see as a last chance to avert a potentially bloody battle for Zaire's capital of five million people.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.

A commander at rebel headquarters in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi said an airlift of rebels and equipment to the towns of Kikwit and Kananga began on Thursday and rebel forces were about to enter Kenge, the biggest town before Kinshasa.

Mobutu's camp says the talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a face-saver to allow the veteran strongman to stand down with dignity.
Kabila insists Mobutu must go. "There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," he said on Wednesday.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, who helped Mandela bring the two sides together, has said there are no conditions for the talks.
"In my view this meeting will produce a process that involves a transfer of power and hopefully a transitional inclusive government," he added on Friday.
Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in August, has towered over what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries virtually since independence from Belgium in 1960.
Opponents denounce rampant corruption and administrative chaos and accuse Mobutu and his entourage of amassing fortunes while the bulk of the population floundered in poverty.
